articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court Officials, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. Concurrently, OFAC designated individuals associated with the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued related General Licenses.

In a separate action, OFAC also announced the removal of a Burma-related designation. These actions reflect a multi-faceted approach to sanctions enforcement and policy adjustments across various geopolitical concerns.

The details of the new General License are expected to clarify permissible activities and may impact various sectors involved in transactions with Russia, requiring careful review by affected parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Issues General Licenses for Iran and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, intensifying pressure on entities and individuals connected to the Iranian regime. These designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. The amended Russia-related license indicates adjustments to existing authorizations, which may affect various economic sectors.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued focus on both Iran and Russia through targeted sanctions and the strategic use of general licenses to manage the scope of restrictions.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The alert likely provides guidance on specific risks or compliance obligations related to Iran, while the amended FAQ offers updated clarifications on existing regulations.

The designations aim to disrupt financial networks and limit the ability of these actors to engage in further illicit activities. This move reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to combating terrorism through economic sanctions.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, based in Sandy, Utah. The enforcement action stems from significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC identified inadequate resources, insufficient staff expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training for employees and directors as key shortcomings. The bank also failed to tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, focusing too narrowly on demand deposit accounts rather than its more dominant credit and charge card products.

These failures led to the bank's inability to timely identify, evaluate, and report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade. The OCC's action, taken in coordination with a concurrent cease-and-desist order from the Federal Reserve, underscores the regulator's commitment to enforcing robust AML compliance.
articles.source: OCC / Traders Union / Cryptonews.net / Banking Dive

articles.headline: BIS Adds Over Three Dozen Entities to Entity List, Citing National Security Concerns
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added more than three dozen companies to its Entity List, effective immediately. These entities, primarily from China (28), but also including those from Belarus, Burma, Pakistan, Russia, and Taiwan, are deemed to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

Nearly half of the newly listed entities, all based in China, were cited for supporting Chinese military modernization and sanctioned parties in Iran. Additionally, a significant number of Chinese and Pakistani entities were added for their involvement in ballistic missile and unsafeguarded nuclear activities.

Several entities in Russia, Belarus, and one in Taiwan were added for supporting Russia's military, while a half-dozen entities were listed for human rights violations in China and Burma, particularly through surveillance programs. This marks the second round of restrictions imposed by the U.S. in as many weeks, emphasizing the need for companies with cross-border dealings to frequently update their counterparty screening.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Legal 500

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
